places.name: Lisbon
places.summary: A hilly city on a wide river mouth, used as a base for slow walks, long afternoons of writing and the planning of slower bus rides.
body: Lisbon is the city I keep returning to for no good reason, which is the best reason. The hills do the work of a gym, the light does the work of a therapist, and the trams do whatever they like.
Most of what is filed here was written elsewhere and edited here, at a café table with a view of a laundry line and a slice of river. It is a good city for finishing things.

projects.title: Pixel Globe
projects.summary: A tiny globe renderer that draws the Earth as dithered pixels: one fragment shader, no textures, and an API small enough to read in an afternoon.

cover.alt: A pixel-art globe lit from the upper left, dithered continents, a faint orbit ring and one cyan location marker

body.text: Pixel Globe started on a flight over Iceland with a laptop at ten percent battery and a simple question: how little code does it take to make a globe that looks hand-drawn? The answer turned out to be one fragment shader, one uniform for rotation and a four-by-four dither matrix, plus a stubborn refusal to load a single texture.
How it works

Each pixel on screen is mapped back to a point on the sphere. Land and sea come from a small noise function instead of an image, then the result is quantised to four tones and ordered-dithered with a Bayer matrix. The cost is the same at any resolution, and the look is the same on a phone and on a wall.
Using it

body.caption: The globe at rest: four tones, one marker.

projects.title: Timetable Diff
projects.summary: A command-line tool that compares two public transit feeds and says, in plain language, which trains were added, retimed or quietly removed.

body.text: I wrote Timetable Diff after arriving at a platform for a train that, according to last month's feed, existed. It does one thing: it takes two GTFS snapshots and tells you what changed, in sentences.
A typical run

body.code:
$ timetable-diff feeds/2026-03.zip feeds/2026-04.zip --route "Ljubljana - Belgrade"

~ 2 trains retimed
  Night 41   Ljubljana 21:40 -> 21:55   (+15 min)
  Night 42   Belgrade  06:12 -> 06:30   (+18 min)
- 1 train removed
  Regional 6012   Zagreb 04:30   (Mon-Fri)
+ 1 train added
  Express 810     Zagreb 05:05   (daily)

body.text: The core

Trips are matched by their identifier and stop sequence, not by their departure time, so a train that merely leaves fifteen minutes later is reported as retimed instead of one train removed and another added. Night trains are the awkward case: they belong to the date they depart, not to the date they arrive.
Changelog

items: 1.2.0: a --since flag compares against the last feed saved in a folder.
1.1.0: night trains are grouped by their departure date, not the calendar day.
1.0.0: stable output format and a JSON mode for scripts.

projects.title: Collide, a label collision engine for maps
projects.summary: A small engine, written in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly, that places thousands of map labels without overlaps and without making the map flicker.

cover.alt: Rectangular map labels with leader lines to anchor points, a few overlapping pairs outlined in cyan

meta.label: Benchmark
meta.value: 12,000 labels in about 4 ms, on a laptop

body.text: Placing labels on a map looks like a layout problem and behaves like a negotiation. Every label wants the best spot, every spot is wanted by three labels, and the moment you move the camera the whole deal has to be renegotiated. Collide is the engine I wrote to make that negotiation fast and, more importantly, stable.
The idea

Labels are ranked by priority, tried in order against up to eight candidate positions, and tested against a spatial grid of the ones already placed. A label that loses is not removed but demoted to a faint state, so it can return as soon as there is room. A short hysteresis window keeps a label from toggling on and off while you pan.

body.alt: Map labels before collision resolution: overlapping boxes outlined in cyan among well-spaced ones
body.caption: Before: twenty labels, several collisions (outlined).

body.alt: The same labels after resolution: no overlap, the moved label framed in cyan
body.caption: After: no overlaps, one label moved to its second-best position.

body.text: The core loop
The grid is a flat vector of cell lists, so a collision test touches at most four cells. On a mid-range laptop that is the difference between a frame budget you notice and one you do not.
Status

The project is paused, not abandoned: the engine works, the benchmarks are honest, and the remaining work is a proper test suite for the awkward cases around the antimeridian. Bug reports with a screenshot are welcome.

projects.title: Weather Ledger
projects.summary: Turns a year of daily weather readings into a pen-plotter drawing: one line per week, one hill per storm. Archived after a year of Wellington winds.

body.text: Weather Ledger began as a way to remember a windy year. Fifty-two lines, one for each week, are drawn from the daily readings of a single station, and the storms show up as hills that hide the lines behind them. It was never meant to be a library, only a small script and a long afternoon at the plotter.
From readings to lines

body.code:
import numpy as np


def weekly_lines(readings, width=297, height=420, step=0.5):
    """One polyline per week: wind speed becomes vertical displacement."""
    weeks = np.array_split(np.asarray(readings, dtype=float), 52)
    x = np.arange(0, width, step)
    lines = []
    for i, week in enumerate(weeks):
        samples = np.interp(x, np.linspace(0, width, len(week)), week)
        y = 10 + i * (height - 20) / 51 - samples * 0.35
        lines.append(np.column_stack([x, y]))
    return lines

body.alt: A pen-plotter drawing of thirty fine lines with a gentle swell, one line in cyan
body.caption: The plot, as drawn: fifty-two weeks of wind.

body.text: Why it is archived

The script did what I wanted, and the year it describes is over. I keep the repository public in case the approach is useful to someone with a different station and a different year, but I no longer accept changes.

articles.title: Night trains through the Balkans
articles.summary: Four nights between Ljubljana, Zagreb, Split and Belgrade by sleeper, and what the timetable never says about couchettes, border stamps and the hour before dawn.

cover.alt: Two railway tracks running to a single lamp on a hazy horizon, drawn in pixels and dithered grey on black, with one cyan signal light

body.text: I did not plan to take the night train four times in one week. The first was a question of arithmetic: a late meeting in Ljubljana, a morning one in Zagreb, and a bed that moved at 120 kilometres an hour was cheaper than a hotel and a taxi. The other three were habit. The fourth went south from Zagreb to the coast at Split, and it is the only one where I slept all the way. By the third night I had stopped checking the time and started checking the sound of the wheels.
Ljubljana, 21:40

The platform is nearly empty and the board still lists the departure in a typeface that has not changed since before I could read. A man sells coffee from a cart that he locks with a bicycle chain. When the train arrives it comes in slowly, almost politely, a long line of blue and grey carriages with their lights already on. My compartment is a couchette for six: three bunks on each side, a folding table, a window that opens exactly as far as a hand.
A night train is the only kind of travel where the destination is allowed to be a surprise to the passenger and not to the driver.
body.cite: Overheard in a corridor, somewhere after midnight

body.alt: An empty platform in perspective, posts with lamps on both sides, one lamp in cyan, faint reflections on the floor
body.caption: The last platform lamps before the dark, Ljubljana, 21:52.

body.text: What I would pack again

items: A scarf, even in March: carriage heating has opinions of its own.
Earplugs and a sleep mask, in that order of importance.
A paper copy of the connection, because phones die in exactly the corridor where the conductor asks.
Small change for the platform tap and a bottle that survives being dropped.
A sandwich that does not need a table.

body.text: Six bunks, five strangers, one ladder. The unspoken rules take about ten minutes to learn: the lowest bunks are for sitting during the day, the middle ones stay folded up until everyone has eaten, and nobody speaks after the conductor has collected the passports. I learned the last one by being the only person still talking.
Belgrade, 06:12

I wake to a grey light and the smell of a coffee I did not make. The river is somewhere to the left, the city is somewhere ahead, and the train stops twice more for reasons nobody explains. A woman across from me folds a blanket into a perfect square, the way you do when you have done it a hundred times. We do not exchange a word, and it is one of the better conversations of the trip.

body.alt: A departures board reduced to bars and cells, several rows outlined in cyan where a time changed
body.caption: A departures board reduced to its bones. The outlined rows are the ones that changed.

articles.title: Rain at the citadel gate
articles.summary: A short note on waiting out a morning downpour under a stone gate in Huế, with three strangers, a thermos of tea and no reason to leave.

body.text: It started at ten past six, and not gently. Four of us stood under the gate, a monk, a schoolboy, a man with a basket of limes and me, watching the moat turn into a second sky. Nobody mentioned the time. Somebody produced a thermos and four small cups, and we drank in a silence that felt less like politeness than like agreement.
When it stopped, forty minutes later, the monk bowed slightly to the weather and walked off, and the rest of us followed in opposite directions.

articles.title: Eleven hours of Atlantic coast, by bus
articles.summary: A slow bus south along the Atlantic coast of Morocco: grilled fish at a roadside stop, a driver who knew every dog by name, and a view that refused to repeat itself.

cover.alt: A dashed road on a cliff above the sea, wave lines receding to a dithered sky, a small cyan bus on the road

body.text: The ticket said eleven hours, which turned out to be an estimate, a hope and a threat at the same time. I had come from Paris by way of a long evening in Lisbon, where I bought a book I would not read and a notebook I would fill, and I boarded the bus in the last hour of the morning with a bag of oranges and no plan for lunch.
The coast, in order

For the first hour the sea is a rumour. You see it as a flatness at the end of a street, then as a band of lighter grey above the rooftops, then, past a roundabout, it is simply there, enormous and unconcerned, and the bus leans toward it like a plant.

body.alt: The coast road mirrored: a dashed road on a cliff on the right, dark sea lines on the left and a cyan bus
body.caption: The road hugs the cliff for most of the afternoon.

body.text: Every stop has its own economy. At the first, women sell bread still warm from a wall oven. At the second, a boy sells phone chargers, then sunglasses, then a single pair of socks, with the same expression. At the third, which is only a wide place in the gravel, the driver gets out, lights nothing, and looks at the water for exactly four minutes.
You are not late. The road is long, that is all.
body.cite: The driver, to a passenger checking her watch

body.text: The day, in numbers

items: Departure at 08:10, which in practice meant 08:50.
First tea at 10:20, poured from a thermos the size of a child.
Lunch at 13:45: grilled fish and bread at a stop with no name.
The long hill at 15:30, where everyone stopped talking.
Arrival at 19:15, in the last of the light.

body.text: I think about that bus more than about most of the places it took me to. Not because anything happened, but because for eleven hours nothing was required of me except to look, and I had forgotten how much of the world is available to anyone willing to sit still on its edge.

body.alt: Stacked swell lines on pale paper, one line in cyan
body.caption: Notes in the margin of the ticket: swell lines, mostly.

body.title: How I plan slow coastal routes
body.description: Timetables, stops and a short list of questions to ask before boarding.

articles.title: Crossing the altiplano at four thousand metres
articles.summary: A bus, a thin coat and a headache: crossing the Andean altiplano in one long day, and what four thousand metres does to appetite, humour and the sense of scale.

cover.alt: Six layers of stair-stepped mountain ridges fading into dithered haze under a small cyan sun

body.text: Altitude is not a number until it becomes a sensation. At 3,400 metres, Cusco is a city with a slight breathlessness and a strong opinion about coca tea. At 4,300, on the highest pass of the road south, it is a pressure behind the eyes and a sudden interest in sitting down.
Before the pass

The bus leaves Cusco at dawn, when the stone streets are still blue and the market women are arranging pyramids of potatoes in colours I did not know a potato could have. We climb through a valley of terraces and eucalyptus, and then, quite abruptly, the trees stop. The land opens into a plateau so wide and so pale that the horizon seems to be a matter of opinion.

body.alt: Five dithered ridge lines on pale paper, the nearest the darkest
body.caption: Ridges behind ridges, as the light flattens toward noon.

body.text: What the body does

items: Appetite goes first, then the ability to estimate distance.
Sentences get shorter. Jokes get worse and are appreciated more.
A walk of two hundred metres feels like a negotiation.
Sleep comes easily and is full of strange, bright dreams.

body.text: The mountain does not care about your plan, but it will let you borrow its silence.
body.cite: A line from my notebook, written with cold hands

body.text: At the pass we stop for ten minutes. People photograph the sign with the number on it, then each other, then nothing in particular. A girl sells hot corn from a bucket. The wind has an edge I will describe for the rest of the year as thin.
After

By late afternoon the plateau tilts and starts to hold water: a lake like a sheet of lead, flocks of small animals the colour of the ground, one lone house with smoke going straight up. I fall asleep for forty minutes and wake with the clear conviction that I have been somewhere, and not merely moved.

body.alt: Close, layered lines of a plateau at night, a cyan line near the bottom
body.caption: Night on the plateau, every line a hill.

body.title: Gear list for high-altitude bus days
body.description: What stayed in the bag, what saved the day, and what I would leave at home.

articles.title: Notes on a thousand-mile train that was meant to take a day and a half, including a long and unplanned stop in a rainstorm
articles.summary: Hanoi to Ho Chi Minh City by rail, written up two years later from a notebook stained with tea: delays, bunks, and the small kindness of strangers with snacks.

body.text: The timetable promised thirty-two hours. The notebook I kept says thirty-nine, which is not a complaint but a measurement. I am writing this up two years after the fact, with the pages still faintly stained with tea, and the memory is kinder than the notebook, which is exactly why I trust the notebook.
Hanoi to Huế: the first night

Hard sleepers, six to a compartment, a ladder that doubles as a shoe rack. A family shares a bag of tangerines with me before the train has cleared the suburbs. I give them my last pack of biscuits, which is a poor trade, and everybody pretends it is an even one.
The stop in the rain

Somewhere south of Huế the rain arrives sideways. The train slows to a walking pace, then stops in a field. For three hours there is nothing to see but water and one patient buffalo, and nothing to do but listen to the carriage settle into a long, collective exhale. At some point the lights go out, and someone starts to hum.

body.alt: A single track running to a lamp at the horizon, ink on pale paper, a cyan signal light
body.caption: A single track, a single lamp: the whole of the afternoon.

body.text: A delay is just the train telling you the country is bigger than your plan.

We reach Da Nang eleven hours late and Ho Chi Minh City on the second morning, in a heat that feels like being returned to a body I had mislaid. I step off the train with sore knees, an empty bag of tangerines and an unreasonable fondness for everyone I have ever shared a compartment with.
What I would do differently

items: Book the lower bunk, and pay no attention to the person who says it is noisier.
Bring more food than seems sensible, and give half of it away.
Keep the notebook dry, or accept the tea.

artworks.title: Signal Study No. 3
artworks.summary: A two-colour risograph print of two overlapping halftone discs, one black and one cyan, studying what happens where two signals cross.

cover.alt: Two overlapping halftone discs, one black and one cyan, with registration marks and a crop frame like a printed proof

meta.label: Medium
meta.value: Two-colour risograph, black and cyan, on 100 g paper

body.text: Signal Study No. 3 is the third in a small series about interference. Two discs of dots, rotated against each other, produce a moiré that neither disc contains on its own, and the print is mostly an excuse to look at that third pattern.

body.alt: Detail of the print: black and cyan halftone dots overlapping at a different angle
body.caption: Detail at 400 percent. The cyan dots are rotated by 31 degrees against the black ones.

body.text: It was printed in two passes at a small studio in Kyoto, black first and cyan second. The registration is deliberately a little loose: the paper moved by about a millimetre between passes, and I decided to keep the drift rather than correct it.
Technical notes

items: Halftone screens at 35 and 45 lines per inch, rotated by 14 and 45 degrees.
Black ink on the first pass, cyan on the second, no varnish.
Each print is numbered in pencil on the lower margin.

artworks.title: Night Platform, Split
artworks.summary: A dithered pixel drawing of a station platform at night, made from a photograph I never took and a memory of lamps that were slightly too bright.

meta.label: Medium
meta.value: Dithered digital print on matte paper

body.text: The platform is empty, the lamps are on, and the last train has either left or not yet arrived. I drew it from memory in a single evening, one lamp at a time, and then let a four-by-four dither decide how much light each part of the floor would keep.

body.text: The second version reverses the plate. On pale paper the lamps become the darkest things in the picture, which is the opposite of how I remember them, and for that reason it is the one I look at longer.

body.text: The light is a schedule: it tells you how long you have been waiting.

artworks.title: Monsoon Index
artworks.summary: A diptych of rooftops in the rain, drawn pixel by pixel in two moods, one dark and one pale, with the same street under both.

cover.alt: Rooftops under a dithered storm sky, thin diagonal rain streaks and ripples on a wet street

body.text: Monsoon Index is a pair of drawings of the same roofline in the same rain: the first at night, the second at the pale hour just after dawn. The rain is one stroke repeated a hundred times, each slightly out of line, and the single cyan stroke is the one I could not stop looking at.

body.alt: Study 1: rooftops and rain under a dithered sky
body.caption: Study 1: rooftops and rain under a dithered sky.

body.alt: Study 2: dark rooftops and rain on pale paper
body.caption: Study 2: dark rooftops and rain on pale paper.

body.text: I made the first study in Huế during a week of storms and the second a few days later in Hội An, where the same weather arrived politer and with a smell of woodsmoke. The title comes from a habit: I kept a daily tally of the hours of rain, and an index seemed the honest name for it.

artworks.title: Altiplano Sediment
artworks.summary: Twelve pen-plotter drawings of stacked contour lines made from notes taken on the Andean plateau: each plate hides the line behind it, like layers of sediment.

cover.alt: Stacked wavy contour lines, each hiding the one behind, with a single cyan line in the lower half

meta.label: Medium
meta.value: Black ink on cotton paper, pen plotter

body.text: The series begins with a long bus ride and a notebook of profiles: the outline of a ridge, redrawn every few minutes as the road moved. Back at the plotter, the profiles became lines, and the lines were stacked from the back of the page to the front, each one erasing what lay behind it.
Four of the twelve plates

body.alt: Plate 1 of the series: eighteen layered lines, a cyan line near the top
body.caption: Plate 1. Eighteen lines, the first drawn in the morning haze.

body.alt: Plate 4 of the series: twenty-two layered lines on pale paper
body.caption: Plate 4. A flatter plate, from the long stretch before the pass.

body.alt: Plate 8 of the series: tall swells in twenty-eight lines
body.caption: Plate 8. The tallest swells of the series, near the highest point.

body.alt: Plate 12 of the series: fourteen lines with large swells, one cyan
body.caption: Plate 12. Fourteen lines and large hills: the last view before the descent.

body.text: Each plate takes about forty minutes to draw, and the plotter's small mistakes, a hesitation at the top of a hill, a slightly doubled line, are part of the work. I keep a log of them, mostly to remind myself that the machine has a hand too.
Land is what remains when you stop describing it.
body.cite: A note pinned above the plotter

items: Collect profiles on the road, by hand, without looking at the paper.
Smooth and resample them into forty-odd points per line.
Stack the lines, back to front, and let each hide the one behind.
Plot in black ink; keep one line in a second colour for the final plate.

body.description: All twelve plates, with the processing notes for each.

poems.title: Layover
poems.summary: Nine hours in an airport between two flights: a poem about benches, announcements and the strange tenderness of being in no place at all.

cover.alt: Short white lines grouped in stanzas, one of them cyan, beside a dithered shadow at the right edge

stanzas: Gate 14 has been closed since noon,
and the sign above it has forgotten
which city it was meant to promise.
I count the windows. I count the planes.
A child lies flat on the carpet
and conducts the whole terminal,
with one finger, as if the announcements, the trolleys and the slow doors were waiting for his count.
Somebody's suitcase turns on the belt
alone, a small patient animal,
making the circuit it was told to make
and finding it enough.
We are all between things here:
between flights, between coffees,
between the person who left
and the one who will land.
The announcer apologises in three languages
and means it in none, and then, once,
in a fourth, quietly, to nobody,
as if to the weather itself.
Outside, the light does that long, flat thing
it does at the edge of the world, and I think:
this is the only hour of the trip that is mine,
and I have spent it waiting for the others.

body.text: Written on a nine-hour layover in Keflavík, on the back of a boarding pass. The last line was the first one I had.

poems.title: Citadel, rain
poems.summary: A three-line poem about a rainy morning at an old gate, where the moat holds on to the sky for a moment before letting it go.

stanzas: Rain on the old gate.
The moat keeps the sky a while,
then lets it go home.

poems.title: Cuesta arriba
poems.summary: Un poema breve sobre subir a cuatro mil metros: la respiración como unidad de medida, y el paisaje como única respuesta.

stanzas: Subir no es un verbo: es una cuenta.
Un paso, un aire. Otro paso, otro aire.
La montaña no cuenta; nos deja contar.
Aquí arriba las palabras pesan menos
y las preguntas pesan más.
Una mujer vende maíz tostado
como quien vende el tiempo en bolsitas.
Y al final del camino no hay nada
que merezca ese nombre:
un viento, una cresta, un perro dormido,
y esta manera de estar vivos
a cuatro mil trescientos metros de todo.

body.text: Escrito en la terraza de un hostal, con un té de coca y las manos frías.

poems.title: Quai de nuit
poems.summary: Un poème sur l'attente d'un train de nuit dans une gare presque vide : les lampes, le froid, et cette façon de partir avant d'être parti.

cover.alt: Short black lines grouped in four stanzas on pale paper, one line in cyan

stanzas: Voie B, vingt-deux heures dix.
Les lampes tiennent le quai
comme des mains tiennent une tasse.
Personne ne parle. Un homme lit
le tableau des départs
comme on relit une lettre
dont on connaît déjà la fin.
Le train n'est pas encore là
mais je suis déjà parti :
c'est ça, une gare,
un endroit pour partir avant le départ.
Puis la lumière jaune, le bruit des freins,
la porte qui s'ouvre sur un couloir étroit
et cette promesse minuscule :
demain, une autre ville, un autre matin.

body.text: Écrit sur un quai, un soir de mars, pendant que le train avait vingt minutes de retard.
